title: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (April 2027) — the second ordinary revision, and the discriminator for whether March is elevated or everything after February is
source: EST: eia.gov/outlooks/steo/release_schedule.php, fetched direct 2026-09-09 (HTTP 200, 54,906 bytes) by the eia-steo-2027-03-09 never-assessed initial research and read from the RAW HTML table, whose 2027 row is "April 2027 | 04/06/2027" with a blank Notes cell; the same page states the release window as 12:00 pm-12:15 pm ET. Reproduces independently from the page's own rule ("the first Tuesday following the first Thursday of each month", a Federal holiday on the preceding Monday pushing the release to Wednesday): 2027-04-01 is a Thursday, the following Tuesday is 04-06, and 2027-04-05 is a Monday that is not a Federal holiday. Filed estimate on the standing EIA grounds — this calendar defines no `confirmed` prefix for the EIA, and a discovering lane never self-confirms an event it found in-sweep — not on date doubt
notes: Discovered during eia-steo-2027-03-09's never-assessed initial research (2026-09-09), off the same raw EIA release-schedule table that dates the March edition. Proposed for one question rather than calendar completeness, and it is the direct successor to the question 03-09 was itself proposed to answer. That session's control passed — a first-print out-year is measurably stickier than a mature one (out/near revision ratio 0.61 and 0.49 for February editions against 0.74, 0.65, 0.66 and 0.70 for March/April/August ones, zero overlap) — but it also found something the sibling chain did not predict: MARCH IS NOT MERELY ORDINARY, IT IS THE LARGEST-MOVING EDITION OF THE EARLY YEAR. On the total US electricity-consumption line the newly-rolled out-year moved -0.31% (Feb 2025) then +0.92% (Mar 2025), and +0.18% (Feb 2026) then +0.37% (Mar 2026) — March is 3.0x and 2.1x February and ranks SECOND OF THE ENTIRE SERIES in both years, against a 0.319% mean for every month from April onward (n=14). Two readings survive that measurement and 04-06 is the only edition that separates them: either MARCH SPECIFICALLY is elevated (the first edition whose previous forecast is itself a revision, and the first to see two months of winter actuals), in which case April reverts to the 0.3% ordinary mean — the 2025 and 2026 April moves were -0.79% and -0.16%, which is consistent but is exactly the two observations that produced the hypothesis — or EVERYTHING AFTER FEBRUARY is elevated and February alone is the quiet month, in which case the sibling's whole stickiness frame is a February artifact rather than a first-print property. The April edition also carries the one calendar feature this lane could not date: eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/ was fetched HTTP 200 on 2026-09-09 and states "Next Release Date: 2027" for the successor to AEO2026 (itself released April 8, 2026) with NO month or day, so an AEO2027 landing near this edition is plausible and undatable today — the Annual Energy Outlook being the one EIA product whose out-year electricity forecast outranks the STEO's for ai-energy-constraint.md. Filed `low` on the sibling entries' reasoning and the measured tape: the pooled STEO-day null reproduced to the cent on a fourth independent pipeline this session (n=24 median |move| below the all-days median in every symbol tested but CRWV). ONE FINDING RECORDED HERE RATHER THAN PROPOSED, so the next lane does not have to rediscover it: per the Fed primary (federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm, fetched 2026-09-09) the 2027 SEP meetings are Mar 16-17, Jun 8-9, Sep 14-15 and Dec 7-8, and the schedule table puts the June and December STEO editions on 06/08/2027 and 12/07/2027 — DAY ONE OF A PROJECTIONS MEETING in both cases, a fifth distinct blackout position after 01-12 (before), 02-09 (none) and 03-09 (inside). Not proposed: the pooled null says a STEO day carries no tape, so the collision is a structural curiosity rather than a research question, and proposing three editions at once would be the calendar completeness this chain deliberately refuses.
